title: Ethics in Real-World Issues
keyIdea: A real-world issue, like whether schools should ban phones, mixes fact questions you can check with values questions you argue with reasons. Think it through by asking who is affected, taking a position with a reason, summing up the other side fairly, and changing your mind if strong new evidence comes in.

kid: Should your school ban phones? In England, the government told schools in 2024 that they should stop phones being used during the school day. Some schools agree. Some people do not. This is a real issue, so it is a good one to practise on.
First, split the questions. How many pupils bring a phone is a fact. You can count it. Is a ban fair is a values question. People can know the same facts and still disagree, so they need reasons.

Next, ask who is affected. A parent may want to reach their child after school. A teacher may want quiet lessons. A pupil with diabetes may need a phone app to check their blood sugar. A good rule thinks about all of them.

Then take a side and give a reason that says who it helps and how. Say the other side's best reason fairly, not a silly version. If strong new evidence turns up, it is fine to change your mind. That is good thinking, not losing.
adult: This fits Key Stage 2 PSHE work on rules, rights and duties. Pupils talk about issues in the news and learn that people hold different views. It also matches the IB Primary Years aim of forming a view and backing it with reasons.

The example is real. In 2024 the Department for Education told schools in England to stop phone use in the school day. It is advice, not law, and it allows exceptions such as medical needs. The evidence is mixed. A 2015 study in four English cities found test scores rose after bans, most for pupils who were behind. A 2025 study of 30 schools found no difference in how well pupils felt.

Common mistakes: treating a values question as if one fact could settle it; giving a popular reason, such as everyone thinks so; attacking a weak version of the other side, called a strawman; and seeing a change of mind as weakness. Ask your child to say the other view in words its supporters would accept.

In the lab your child sorts fact and values questions and matches reasons to a pupil, a parent, a teacher and a pupil with diabetes. They place a marker on a line from against to for and back it with a reason. Then they pick the fair summary of each side and sort new evidence.

familyTip: Pick a rule from the news or from home, such as screen time at weekends. Each take a side and give one reason about who it helps. Then swap: each of you sums up the other side so fairly that the other person says, yes, that is what I mean. Finish by asking what new fact could change your mind.

visual.caption: Can you check it, or do people argue it with reasons? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: How many cars pass the school each morning?
Should cars be banned outside the gate?
Is it fair that older pupils go first at lunch?
What does the school rule say about uniform?
Should pupils choose their own uniform?

lab.caption: Flagship lab: on the school phone ban, split fact from values, match reasons to people, take a side, be fair and sort evidence.

practice.prompt: In a survey, {n} out of 30 pupils in a class say phones distract them. Does that number settle whether a ban is fair?
choices: No, it is useful evidence, but fairness also needs reasons about values
Yes, numbers always settle it
Yes, if the number is big enough
practice.hint: Is fair a word you can count, or a word you argue about?
practice.explain: The survey is a fact that helps the argument, but fair is a values question, so it also needs reasons about who is helped and who loses out.

practice.prompt: A class lists {a} reasons for a ban and {b} reasons against it. How many reasons is that in total to weigh?
practice.hint: Add the reasons on both sides.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} reasons. The number is only a start: one strong reason can matter more than several weak ones.

practice.prompt: Which is the fairest summary of people who are against a phone ban?
choices: Some families want children to have a phone for the way home
They only care about games
They have no reasons at all
practice.hint: Would people on that side agree with your summary?
practice.explain: Families wanting a phone for the way home is a real reason that supporters would accept, so it is a fair summary, not a strawman.

practice.prompt: Zara was for a ban. Then she read a study showing a ban did not help wellbeing, so she changed her view a little. What does this show?
choices: Good thinking: she let new evidence move her
Weakness: she should never change her mind
She was wrong to read the study
practice.hint: What should a good thinker do with strong new evidence?
practice.explain: Weighing new evidence and adjusting your view is good thinking. Holding on no matter what is not.

pool.prompt: In a school of {a} pupils, {b} pupils need a phone for a medical reason. How many pupils would a full ban with no exceptions affect without any problem?
pool.hint: Take the pupils with a medical need away from the total.
pool.explain: {a} - {b} = {=a-b} pupils. The other {b} would be put at risk, which is why fair rules can have exceptions.

pool.prompt: {n} pupils say a phone ban is right because everyone they know agrees. What kind of reason is that?
choices: A popularity reason, which is weak on its own
The strongest kind of reason
A fact that settles it
pool.hint: Does it say who is helped and how?
pool.explain: Lots of people agreeing does not explain who is helped or harmed, so on its own it is a weak, popularity reason.

pool.prompt: Which of these is a values question?
choices: Should phones be allowed at break time?
How many pupils own a phone?
What time does school finish?
pool.hint: Look for words like should, fair or right.
pool.explain: Should phones be allowed asks what is right, so people argue it with reasons. The others can be checked.

choices: A weak, twisted version of someone's view that is easy to knock down
The best version of someone's view
A fact that proves you right
pool.hint: Think about the unfair summaries in the lab.
pool.explain: A strawman twists the other side into something silly. A fair thinker sums up their best reason instead.

pool.prompt: Which is the strongest reason for a phone ban?
choices: Fewer phones buzzing means fewer distractions in lessons
My friends all think so
Phones are annoying
pool.hint: Which reason says who it helps and how?
pool.explain: Fewer distractions explains who is helped and how, so it is stronger than a feeling or a popular view.

pool.prompt: Who is affected by a school phone rule?
choices: Pupils, parents and teachers
Only pupils
Only the head teacher
pool.hint: Think about the four people in the lab.
pool.explain: A phone rule affects pupils, parents who want to reach them and teachers who run lessons, so a fair rule thinks about all of them.

pool.prompt: One study found test scores went up after phone bans. What is the best way to use this?
choices: As one piece of evidence, alongside other studies
As proof that ends the argument
Ignore it because it is only numbers
pool.hint: Is one study the last word?
pool.explain: One study is useful evidence, but other studies found different things, so weigh it with the rest.

pool.prompt: Before you argue against someone's view, what should you be able to do?
choices: Say their view in a way they would call fair
Prove they are silly
Talk louder than them
pool.hint: Would they agree with your summary?
pool.explain: If you can say their view fairly, you understand it, and your own argument gets stronger.
